**Surah al-Ma'un, seven verses, Meccan**

[Page 104]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿Have you seen the one who denies the Recompense?﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿Have you seen the one who denies the Recompense?﴾ On it are several issues:

**First issue:** Some read "أرَيْتَ" (*arayta*) with the hamza omitted. Al-Zajjaj said: "This is not the preferred reading, because the hamza is dropped only from the imperfect, as in يَرى (*yara*), أرى (*ara*) and تَرى (*tara*). As for رَأيْتُ (*ra'aytu*), the Arabs are not reliably reported to say رَيْتُ (*raytu*). However, since the interrogative particle comes at the beginning of the sentence, dropping the hamza was made easier. A parallel is the line:

*He cried, "Have you seen, or heard of, a shepherd who returned to the udder what he had milked into the vessels?"*

Ibn Mas'ud read "أرَأيْتَكَ" (*ara'aytaka*), with the added particle of address, as in the words of God: ﴿Have you seen this one whom You have honored above me?﴾ [al-Isra' 17:62]."

**Second issue:** The phrase "أرَأيْتَ" (*ara'ayta*) means: "Do you know who the one who denies the Recompense is? If you do not know him, he is: ﴿the one who repulses the orphan﴾."

Know that although this expression is in the form of a question, its purpose is to emphasize amazement, as when you say: "Have you seen so-and-so, what he has committed, and why he has put himself at risk?" It has then been said that it is addressed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It has also been said that it is addressed to every person of intellect, meaning: "Have you seen, O intelligent one, this one who denies the Religion after its proofs have become manifest and its clarity evident, would he do this without a purpose? How is it becoming for an intelligent person to bring eternal punishment upon himself without a purpose, or for the sake of this world? How is it becoming for an intelligent person to sell what is abundant and lasting for what is scant and perishing?"

**Third issue:** There are two opinions on the verse.

The first is that it refers to a specific individual. On this view, they mentioned several persons. Ibn Jurayj said: it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan, who would slaughter two camels every week, and an orphan came to him asking for meat, and he struck him with his staff. Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi, whose characteristic was combining the denial of the Day of Resurrection with committing ugly deeds. al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. al-Mawardi related that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. It is also narrated that "he was the guardian of an orphan, and the orphan came to him, naked, asking him for something from his own property, and he pushed him away and paid him no regard, so the boy despaired. The notables of Quraysh said to him: 'Tell Muhammad to intercede for you.' Their purpose was mockery, and the orphan did not realize this. He went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him for this. He, peace and blessings be upon him, never turned away anyone in need, so he went with him to Abu Jahl. Abu Jahl welcomed him and offered the orphan the money. Quraysh reproached him, saying: 'You have inclined.' He said: 'No, by God, I have not inclined. But I saw to his right and to his left a spear, and I feared that if I did not respond to him, he would thrust it into me.'" It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed concerning a hypocrite who combined stinginess with ostentation.

The second opinion is that it is general, applying to everyone who denies the Day of Religion. This is because a person's undertaking of acts of obedience and his abstention from what is forbidden only occur out of desire for reward and fear of punishment. When someone denies the Resurrection, he gives up nothing of his desires and pleasures. Thus it is established that denial of the Resurrection is like the root of all kinds of disbelief and disobedience.

**Fourth issue:** There are several interpretations (*tafsir*, here meaning explanation) of the word "al-Din" (the Religion, the Recompense):

The first: the intended meaning is one who denies the Religion itself and Islam, either because he denied the Creator, or because he denied prophethood, or because he denied the Return, or some of the laws. If it is asked: how can it be understood in this sense, when everyone must have some religion? The answer has several aspects:

The first: the absolute "dīn" in the terminology of the people of Islam and the Qur'an is Islam. God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the religion with God is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:19]. As for other creeds, they are not called "dīn" except with some qualification, such as the religion of the Christians and the Jews.

The second: it may be said that these false doctrines are not a religion, because religion is submission to God, whereas these doctrines are only submission to desire or to doubt.

The third, which is the view of most exegetes: the intended meaning is "Have you seen the one who denies the Reckoning and the Recompense?" They said: interpreting it in this sense is preferable, because one who denies Islam may perform praiseworthy deeds and avoid blameworthy ones when he acknowledges the Resurrection and the Resurrection of the dead. But one who undertakes every ugly act without any concern is none other than one who denies the Resurrection and the Day of Judgment.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 107, verses 2–5:**

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So that is the one who repulses the orphan﴾ ﴿and does not urge the feeding of the needy﴾.

Know that God, exalted is He, mentioned two attributes in describing the one who denies the Din (religion, judgment):

The first belongs to the category of actions, and it is His saying: ﴿So that is the one who repulses the orphan﴾.

The second belongs to the category of omissions, and it is His saying: ﴿and does not urge the feeding of the needy﴾. The fa' in His saying "fa-dhalika" (so that) indicates causation. That is, since he is a disbeliever who denies, his disbelief is the cause of his repulsing the orphan. He limited the description to these two only in the sense that what issues from one who denies the Din is nothing but these, because we know that the one who denies the Din is not limited to these two. Rather, they are given as examples. It is as if God mentioned one example in each of the two categories, as an alert, through which He points to all the other ugly deeds. Or it is because these two traits, just as they are reprehensible and disapproved by the Shari'ah, are also disapproved by manliness and humanity.

As for His saying ﴿repulses the orphan﴾, the meaning is that he pushes him away with violence and harshness, like His saying: ﴿On the Day they will be pushed (yuda'ayna) into the fire of Hell with a violent pushing﴾ [al-Tur: 13]. The sum of what is meant by repulsing the orphan comprises several matters:

The first: pushing him away from his right and his property by oppression.

The second: abandoning kindness toward him, although kindness is not obligatory. A person may be blamed for abandoning voluntary acts (nawafil, supererogatory deeds), especially if this is attributed to hypocrisy and lack of religion.

[Page 106]

The third: he rebukes him, beats him, and treats him with contempt. It has been recited as "yada'" (he leaves/abandons him), meaning he leaves him, and does not invite him with an invitation, that is, he invites all the strangers and leaves the orphan out, even though he (peace be upon him) said: "There is no table more excellent than a table on which there is an orphan." It has also been recited as "yad'u al-yatim" (he invites the orphan), meaning he invites him for show, then does not feed him. He only invites him for servitude, or by compulsion, or by arrogance.

Know that in His saying "yaduʿʿu" (ﷺ) with the doubled ʿayn (shaddah), there is a benefit: "yaduʿʿu" with the shaddah means that he is habitually doing this. So the threat does not apply to the one in whom this occurs and who then regrets it. A similar example is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who avoid the major sins and the shameful deeds, except for minor lapses (al-lamam)﴾ [al-Najm: 32]. The sin of the believer is called lamam because it is like a phantom and an image that passes and does not remain, since the believer, as soon as he is finished with the sin, regrets it. The one who denies is only the one who persists in sin.

As for His saying ﴿and does not urge the feeding of the needy﴾, there are two interpretations:

The first: he does not urge himself to feed the needy. The attribution of the food to the needy indicates that this food is the right of the needy. It is as if he withheld from the needy what is his right, and this indicates the extreme of his miserliness, hardness of heart, and baseness of nature.

The second: he does not urge others to feed that needy person, because he does not believe in any reward for that act. The sum is that God, exalted is He, made the knowledge of denying the Resurrection the cause of boldness in harming the weak and withholding good. That is, if he believed in recompense and were certain of the threat, this would not have proceeded from him. So the locus of the sin is denial of the Resurrection. Here there are two questions:

The first question: Does not a person in many circumstances refrain from urging, and is not sinful? The answer: Because someone else takes his place, or because his word would not be accepted, or because of another harm he anticipates. But here he mentioned that he does not do this, except (illa) because he is a denier of the Din.

The second question: Why did He not say "and does not feed the needy"? The answer: If he withholds the orphan's right, how would he feed the needy from his own wealth? Rather, he is stingy with the wealth of others, and this is the ultimate in baseness. So being stingy with his own wealth is all the more so. Its opposite, in praise of the believers, is: ﴿and they enjoin one another to mercy﴾ [al-Balad: 17], ﴿and they enjoin one another to truth﴾ [al-'Asr: 3], ﴿and they enjoin one another to patience﴾ [al-'Asr: 3]. ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾ ﴿who are heedless of their prayer﴾.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾ ﴿who are heedless of their prayer﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

Issue one: Regarding how this verse connects with what precedes it, there are several views:

The first: that he does not do the harming of the orphan and the withholding of food as evidence of hypocrisy. Prayer, without humility, and humility being better, indicates hypocrisy. This is because harming and withholding benefit is a dealing with the created, whereas prayer is a service to the Creator.

The second: as if, when He mentioned harming the orphan and abandoning urging feeding, someone was to say: "Does not prayer forbid indecency and wrongdoing?" So He said to him: "How can prayer forbid this reprehensible act, when it is made of pure show and heedlessness?"

The third: as if He is saying: his boldness in harming the orphan and his abandonment of urging feeding is a shortcoming in what pertains to compassion for God's creatures, and his heedlessness in prayer is a shortcoming in what pertains to glorifying God's command. So when the shortcoming occurred in both matters, his wretchedness was complete. Therefore He said: "woe." Know that this expression is only used in the case of a grave crime, as in His saying: ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 1], ﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79], ﴿Woe to every slanderer and backbiter﴾ [al-Humazah: 1]. It is also reported that everyone wails in the Fire according to his crime: one says, "Woe is me because of love of rank," another says, "Woe is me because of tribal zealotry (al-hamiyyah al-jahiliyyah)," and another says, "Woe is me because of my prayer." Therefore, it is recommended upon hearing such a verse that a person say: "Woe is me, unless I am forgiven."

Issue two: The verse indicates the occurrence of a great threat for doing three matters:

The first: heedlessness toward prayer.

The second: doing showing-off (riya').

The third: withholding al-ma'un (small necessary kindnesses). All of these are from the category of sins, and a person does not become a hypocrite by them. So why did God decree such a threat for the doer of these acts? Because of this difficulty, the exegetes gave several answers:

The first: that His saying ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾ means: woe to those of the hypocrites who pray, who commit these acts. According to this reading, the verse indicates that the disbeliever has additional punishment because of his boldness in prohibitions of the Shari'ah and his abandonment of the obligations of the Shari'ah. This indicates the soundness of the view of al-Shafi'i: that disbelievers are addressed concerning the secondary branches of the Shari'ahs. This answer is the one relied upon.

The second: what 'Ata' reported from Ibn 'Abbas, that if God had said "in their prayer they are heedless," this threat would apply to believers. But He said ﴿from their prayer they are heedless﴾. The one who is heedless of the prayer is the one who does not remember it and is empty of it. This view is weak, because heedlessness toward prayer cannot be interpreted as abandoning prayer, since He affirmed prayer for them by His saying ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾. Also, heedlessness toward prayer in the sense of abandonment is not hypocrisy or disbelief, so the difficulty returns. The first objection can be answered by saying that He judged them as praying according to the outward form, and that they forgot the prayer altogether according to its inner meaning, as He said: ﴿And when they stand up to prayer, they stand lazily, showing off to people, and they do not remember God except a little﴾ [al-Nisa': 142]. The second objection can be answered by saying that forgetting the prayer is to remain forgetful of the remembrance of God throughout all the parts of the prayer. This only proceeds from the hypocrite who believes that there is no benefit in prayer. As for the Muslim who believes that prayer has an essential benefit, it is impossible that he would not remember the matter of the Din, the reward and the punishment, in any part of the prayer. Rather, it may happen to him that he becomes heedless in the prayer in the sense that he becomes inattentive in some parts of it. So it is established that heedlessness within the prayer is among the acts of the believer, whereas heedlessness toward the prayer is among the acts of the disbeliever.

The third: that the meaning of "sahun" (heedless) is that they do not attend to the times of their prayers or their conditions. Its meaning is that he does not care whether he prays or does not pray. This is the view of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Masruq, al-Hasan, and Muqatil.

Issue three: They differed concerning the forgetfulness (sahw) of the Messenger (ﷺ) in his prayer. Many scholars said: he (ﷺ) did not forget, but God permitted him that act so that he would do what the forgetful person does, and that would become an explanation of that Shari'ah through action, and explanation through action is stronger. Then, supposing forgetfulness did occur from him, forgetfulness is of several kinds:

The first: the forgetfulness of the Messenger and the Companions, which is made good sometimes by the prostration of forgetfulness (sujud al-sahw) and sometimes by the sunan (recommended practices) and the nawafil.

The second: what occurs in the prayer of heedlessness and absence of the presence of the knowledge and the intentions.

The third: abandonment without making up for it, and letting it pass its time. Among this is the prayer of the hypocrite, which is worse than abandoning prayer, because he mocks the Din by that prayer.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who show off﴾, know that the difference between the hypocrite and the one who shows off is: the hypocrite is the one who displays faith while concealing disbelief, whereas the one who shows off displays what is not in his heart of extra humility, so that whoever sees him believes he is pious. Or you may say: the hypocrite does not pray in secret, whereas the one who shows off has a prayer that is better in the presence of people.

Know that it is obligatory to make the obligatory acts of prayer and zakat apparent, because they are the symbols of Islam, and whoever abandons them deserves cursing. Therefore it is necessary to negate the suspicion through making them apparent. Concealment is only for the supererogatory acts, unless one makes the supererogatory acts apparent so that he may be followed. It is reported from some of them that he saw in the mosque a man performing a prostration of gratitude (sujud al-shukr) and prolonging it, so he said: "How excellent this would be if it were in your house!" Nevertheless, they said: one should not abandon the supererogatory acts out of shame, nor perform them out of showing off, and it is rarely easy to avoid showing off. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Showing off is more hidden than the crawling of a black ant on a black stone in a dark night."

If it is said: What is the meaning of al-muraa'ah (showing off)?

We say: it is a form of mufa'alah from al-ira'ah (showing), because the one who shows off shows people his deed, and they show him praise for it and admiration of it.

The first: pushing him away from his right and his property by oppression.

The second: abandoning kindness toward him, although kindness is not obligatory. A person may be blamed for abandoning voluntary acts (nawafil, supererogatory deeds), especially if this is attributed to hypocrisy and lack of religion.

The third: he rebukes him, beats him, and treats him with contempt. The first: he does not urge himself to feed the needy. The attribution of the food to the needy indicates that this food is the right of the needy. It is as if he withheld from the needy what is his right, and this indicates the extreme of his miserliness, hardness of heart, and baseness of nature.

The second: he does not urge others to feed that needy person, because he does not believe in any reward for that act. The sum is that God, exalted is He, made the knowledge of denying the Resurrection the cause of boldness in harming the weak and withholding good. That is, if he believed in recompense and were certain of the threat, this would not have proceeded from him. So the locus of the sin is denial of the Resurrection. Here there are two questions:

The first question: Does not a person in many circumstances refrain from urging, and is not sinful? The answer: Because someone else takes his place, or because his word would not be accepted, or because of another harm he anticipates. But here he mentioned that he does not do this, except (illa) because he is a denier of the Din.

The second question: Why did He not say "and does not feed the needy"? The answer: If he withholds the orphan's right, how would he feed the needy from his own wealth? * * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾ ﴿who are heedless of their prayer﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

Issue one: Regarding how this verse connects with what precedes it, there are several views:

The first: that he does not do the harming of the orphan and the withholding of food as evidence of hypocrisy. Prayer, without humility, and humility being better, indicates hypocrisy. This is because harming and withholding benefit is a dealing with the created, whereas prayer is a service to the Creator.

The second: as if, when He mentioned harming the orphan and abandoning urging feeding, someone was to say: "Does not prayer forbid indecency and wrongdoing?" So He said to him: "How can prayer forbid this reprehensible act, when it is made of pure show and heedlessness?"

The third: as if He is saying: his boldness in harming the orphan and his abandonment of urging feeding is a shortcoming in what pertains to compassion for God's creatures, and his heedlessness in prayer is a shortcoming in what pertains to glorifying God's command. So when the shortcoming occurred in both matters, his wretchedness was complete. Therefore He said: "woe." Know that this expression is only used in the case of a grave crime, as in His saying: ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 1], ﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79], ﴿Woe to every slanderer and backbiter﴾ [al-Humazah: 1]. It is also reported that everyone wails in the Fire according to his crime: one says, "Woe is me because of love of rank," another says, "Woe is me because of tribal zealotry (al-hamiyyah al-jahiliyyah)," and another says, "Woe is me because of my prayer." Therefore, it is recommended upon hearing such a verse that a person say: "Woe is me, unless I am forgiven."

Issue two: The verse indicates the occurrence of a great threat for doing three matters:

The first: heedlessness toward prayer.

The second: doing showing-off (riya').

The third: withholding al-ma'un (small necessary kindnesses). All of these are from the category of sins, and a person does not become a hypocrite by them. So why did God decree such a threat for the doer of these acts? Because of this difficulty, the exegetes gave several answers:

The first: that His saying ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾ means: woe to those of the hypocrites who pray, who commit these acts. According to this reading, the verse indicates that the disbeliever has additional punishment because of his boldness in prohibitions of the Shari'ah and his abandonment of the obligations of the Shari'ah. This indicates the soundness of the view of al-Shafi'i: that disbelievers are addressed concerning the secondary branches of the Shari'ahs. This answer is the one relied upon.

The second: what 'Ata' reported from Ibn 'Abbas, that if God had said "in their prayer they are heedless," this threat would apply to believers. But He said ﴿from their prayer they are heedless﴾. The one who is heedless of the prayer is the one who does not remember it and is empty of it. This view is weak, because heedlessness toward prayer cannot be interpreted as abandoning prayer, since He affirmed prayer for them by His saying ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾. Also, heedlessness toward prayer in the sense of abandonment is not hypocrisy or disbelief, so the difficulty returns. The first objection can be answered by saying that He judged them as praying according to the outward form, and that they forgot the prayer altogether according to its inner meaning, as He said: ﴿And when they stand up to prayer, they stand lazily, showing off to people, and they do not remember God except a little﴾ [al-Nisa': 142]. The second objection can be answered by saying that forgetting the prayer is to remain forgetful of the remembrance of God throughout all the parts of the prayer. This only proceeds from the hypocrite who believes that there is no benefit in prayer. As for the Muslim who believes that prayer has an essential benefit, it is impossible that he would not remember the matter of the Din, the reward and the punishment, in any part of the prayer. Rather, it may happen to him that he becomes heedless in the prayer in the sense that he becomes inattentive in some parts of it. So it is established that heedlessness within the prayer is among the acts of the believer, whereas heedlessness toward the prayer is among the acts of the disbeliever.

The third: that the meaning of "sahun" (heedless) is that they do not attend to the times of their prayers or their conditions. Its meaning is that he does not care whether he prays or does not pray. This is the view of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Masruq, al-Hasan, and Muqatil.

Issue three: They differed concerning the forgetfulness (sahw) of the Messenger (ﷺ) in his prayer. Many scholars said: he (ﷺ) did not forget, but God permitted him that act so that he would do what the forgetful person does, and that would become an explanation of that Shari'ah through action, and explanation through action is stronger. Then, supposing forgetfulness did occur from him, forgetfulness is of several kinds:

The first: the forgetfulness of the Messenger and the Companions, which is made good sometimes by the prostration of forgetfulness (sujud al-sahw) and sometimes by the sunan (recommended practices) and the nawafil.

The second: what occurs in the prayer of heedlessness and absence of the presence of the knowledge and the intentions.

The third: abandonment without making up for it, and letting it pass its time. Among this is the prayer of the hypocrite, which is worse than abandoning prayer, because he mocks the Din by that prayer.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who show off﴾, know that the difference between the hypocrite and the one who shows off is: the hypocrite is the one who displays faith while concealing disbelief, whereas the one who shows off displays what is not in his heart of extra humility, so that whoever sees him believes he is pious. Or you may say: the hypocrite does not pray in secret, whereas the one who shows off has a prayer that is better in the presence of people.

Know that it is obligatory to make the obligatory acts of prayer and zakat apparent, because they are the symbols of Islam, and whoever abandons them deserves cursing. Therefore it is necessary to negate the suspicion through making them apparent. Concealment is only for the supererogatory acts, unless one makes the supererogatory acts apparent so that he may be followed. It is reported from some of them that he saw in the mosque a man performing a prostration of gratitude (sujud al-shukr) and prolonging it, so he said: "How excellent this would be if it were in your house!" Nevertheless, they said: one should not abandon the supererogatory acts out of shame, nor perform them out of showing off, and it is rarely easy to avoid showing off. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Showing off is more hidden than the crawling of a black ant on a black stone in a dark night."

If it is said: What is the meaning of al-muraa'ah (showing off)?

We say: it is a form of mufa'alah from al-ira'ah (showing), because the one who shows off shows people his deed, and they show him praise for it and admiration of it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 107, verse 6–7:

Know that His saying: ﴿Who are heedless of their prayer﴾ indicates two matters: delaying it beyond its time (al-ikhraj 'an al-waqt), and a person being heedless within it. His saying: ﴿Who make show of their deeds﴾ indicates ostentation (al-muraa'a). Thus it is clear that the prayer must be free of these three states.

Then, when He explained the matter of prayer, He followed it with mention of charity (al-sila't), saying: ﴿and refuse [common] assistance﴾. Regarding this there are several opinions:

The first, which is the view of Abu Bakr, Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Hanafiyyah, Ibn Amr, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Dahhak, is that it means zakah. In the hadith of Ubayy: "Whoever recites the surah (Ara'ayta), Allah will forgive him if he has been one who pays zakah." This suggests that (al-ma'un) is zakah. Also, since Allah mentioned it right after the prayer, the apparent meaning is that it is zakah.

The second view, which is the view of most exegetes, is that (al-ma'un) is the name for what is not usually withheld, and what both the poor and the rich ask for; whoever withholds it is attributed with bad character and base nature, such as the axe, the cooking pot, the bucket, the flint, the sieve and the adze. It also includes salt, water and fire, for it has been narrated: "Three things it is not lawful to withhold: water, fire and salt." Among this is that your neighbour asks to bake in your oven, or to place his goods with you for a day or half a day. The proponents of this view said: al-ma'un is fa'ul from al-ma'n, which is a small amount; and from it comes "he has neither much (sa'nah) nor little (ma'nah)," meaning much and not little. Zakah was called ma'un because a quarter of a tenth is taken from wealth, so it is a small part of a large amount. And what is lent in custom, such as the axe and the knife, is called ma'un. On this interpretation, the meaning of the verse is a rebuke against miserliness with these small things, for miserliness with them is at the extreme of baseness and meanness, and the hypocrites were like this, as in His saying: ﴿Those who are stingy and enjoin stinginess upon people﴾ [al-Hadid: 24], and He said: ﴿withholding from good, transgressing, sinful﴾ [al-Qalam: 12]. The scholars said: among the virtues is that a man should keep in his home a surplus of what his neighbours need, so that he lends it to them and does not limit himself to what is obligatory.

The third view: al-Farra' said: I heard some of the Arabs say: al-ma'un is water, and he recited to me concerning it:

"His camel spits out al-ma'un, spitting [it out]."

Perhaps He singled it out for this because it is the most precious of what is missing and the cheapest of what is available, and the first thing the people of the Fire ask for is water, as He said: ﴿Pour upon us some of the water﴾ [al-A'raf: 50], and the first pleasure the people of Paradise find is water, as He said: ﴿And their Lord gave them drink﴾ [al-Insan: 21].

The fourth view: (al-ma'un) is good compliance (husn al-inqiyad). It is said: "Train your camel until it gives you al-ma'un," meaning until it gives you obedience.

Page 109

Know that it is better to interpret it as every act of obedience that is light to perform, for it is more beneficial. Then the scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) said regarding the coherence between His saying "those who make show" and His saying ﴿and refuse [common] assistance﴾: it is as if He, exalted, says: the prayer is for Me and the common assistance is for creation; so what is due to Me they display before creation, and what is the right of creation they conceal from them. It is as though he treats creation and the Lord only in reverse. If it is said: why did Allah not mention the disbeliever by name? If you say it is to conceal him, I say: why did He not conceal Adam, but said: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord﴾?

The answer: He mentioned Adam's slip, but after his death, coupled with repentance, so that it would be a kindness to his descendants: that he was expelled from Paradise because of a minor sin, so how can they hope to enter with a major sin? Also, describing that slip is an elevation for him, for he was a man from whom only that one slip proceeded, and then he repented from it with such repentance.

Let us conclude the tafsir of this surah with supplication: Our God, this surah is about the hypocrites, and the surah after it describes Muhammad (ﷺ). Although we have not reached Muhammad, peace be upon him, and his companions in obedience, we have not reached these hypocrites in evil deeds. So pardon us by Your grace, O Most Merciful of the merciful. May Allah bless our master Muhammad, and his family, companions, and grant them peace.

Zakah was called ma'un because a quarter of a tenth is taken from wealth, so it is a small part of a large amount. And what is lent in custom, such as the axe and the knife, is called ma'un. On this interpretation, the meaning of the verse is a rebuke against miserliness with these small things, for miserliness with them is at the extreme of baseness and meanness, and the hypocrites were like this, as in His saying: ﴿Those who are stingy and enjoin stinginess upon people﴾ [al-Hadid: 24], and He said: ﴿withholding from good, transgressing, sinful﴾ [al-Qalam: 12]. The scholars said: among the virtues is that a man should keep in his home a surplus of what his neighbours need, so that he lends it to them and does not limit himself to what is obligatory.

The third view: al-Farra' said: I heard some of the Arabs say: al-ma'un is water, and he recited to me concerning it:

"His camel spits out al-ma'un, spitting [it out]."

Perhaps He singled it out for this because it is the most precious of what is missing and the cheapest of what is available, and the first thing the people of the Fire ask for is water, as He said: ﴿Pour upon us some of the water﴾ [al-A'raf: 50], and the first pleasure the people of Paradise find is water, as He said: ﴿And their Lord gave them drink﴾ [al-Insan: 21].

The fourth view: (al-ma'un) is good compliance (husn al-inqiyad). It is said: "Train your camel until it gives you al-ma'un," meaning until it gives you obedience.

Page 109

Know that it is better to interpret it as every act of obedience that is light to perform, for it is more beneficial. Then the scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) said regarding the coherence between His saying "those who make show" and His saying ﴿and refuse [common] assistance﴾: it is as if He, exalted, says: the prayer is for Me and the common assistance is for creation; so what is due to Me they display before creation, and what is the right of creation they conceal from them. It is as though he treats creation and the Lord only in reverse. If it is said: why did Allah not mention the disbeliever by name? If you say it is to conceal him, I say: why did He not conceal Adam, but said: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord﴾?

The answer: He mentioned Adam's slip, but after his death, coupled with repentance, so that it would be a kindness to his descendants: that he was expelled from Paradise because of a minor sin, so how can they hope to enter with a major sin? Also, describing that slip is an elevation for him, for he was a man from whom only that one slip proceeded, and then he repented from it with such repentance.

Let us conclude the tafsir of this surah with supplication: Our God, this surah is about the hypocrites, and the surah after it describes Muhammad (ﷺ). Although we have not reached Muhammad, peace be upon him, and his companions in obedience, we have not reached these hypocrites in evil deeds. So pardon us by Your grace, O Most Merciful of the merciful. May Allah bless our master Muhammad, and his family, companions, and grant them peace.
